claim: NINL is a dynein activating adaptor that has evolved under recurrent positive (diversifying) selection in primates.
source: Unique among genes encoding components of active dynein complexes, NINL has evolved under recurrent positive (diversifying) selection, particularly in its carboxy-terminal cargo-binding region.
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis data presented in Figure 1B showing NINL has elevated dN/dS and significant p-value for positive selection compared to other dynein components, and by codon-based analyses identifying 30 codons under positive selection (Figure 1C, Supplementary files 1-3).

claim: NINL knockout cells exhibit an impaired response to interferon, resulting in increased permissiveness to viral replication.
source: Consistent with a role for NINL in host immunity, we demonstrate that NINL knockout cells exhibit an impaired response to interferon, resulting in increased permissiveness to viral replication.
evidence: Demonstrated by viral replication assays showing that NINL KO cells have significantly reduced antiviral effects of IFNα pretreatment compared to WT cells for VSV, SinV, and CVB3 (Figure 2B-D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Proteases encoded by diverse picornaviruses and coronaviruses cleave and disrupt NINL function in a host- and virus-specific manner.
source: Moreover, we show that proteases encoded by diverse picornaviruses and coronaviruses cleave and disrupt NINL function in a host- and virus-specific manner.
evidence: Supported by cleavage assays showing CVB3 3Cpro cleaves NINL at three sites (Q231, Q827, Q1032) that vary among primates (Figure 5), and that diverse viral proteases cleave NINL with variable efficiency and site preference (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Functional disruption demonstrated by peroxisome trafficking assays (Figures 6-7).

claim: Most dynein, dynactin, and activating adaptor genes are extremely well conserved with dN/dS values of <0.1.
source: Consistent with the critical role of dynein-mediated intracellular transport, most genes we analyzed were extremely well conserved with dN/dS values of <0.1, while one dynein activating adaptor, NINL, showed an elevated rate compared to the rest (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1 comparing dN/dS values across 23 dynein/dynactin genes and 13 activating adaptor genes.

claim: 24 of 30 codons showing signatures of positive selection in NINL are located in the carboxy-terminal cargo-binding region rather than the dynein/dynactin-binding region.
source: Most (24 of 30) of these codons are excluded from the known dynein/dynactin-binding region of NINL (residues 1–702) (Redwine et al., 2017) and instead are located in the carboxy-terminal region of the protein that is expected to interact with cargo (residues 703–1382).
evidence: Supported by codon-based evolutionary analyses using PAML, FEL, and MEME methods identifying specific codons under positive selection (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2), and domain-specific analyses showing no positive selection in N-terminus but significant positive selection in C-terminus (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 3).

claim: The antiviral effect of IFNα is significantly attenuated in NINL KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: In contrast, we observed that the effect of IFNα was significantly attenuated in NINL KO cells, where we found that IFNα pretreatment reduced VSV replication <10-fold (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by viral replication assays showing >100-fold decrease in VSV replication in WT cells with IFNα pretreatment versus <10-fold decrease in NINL KO cells (Figure 2B).

claim: VSV replication is higher in NINL KO cell lines compared to WT even in the absence of IFN.
source: We also noted that VSV replication was higher in NINL KO cell lines compared to WT even in the absence of IFN, which may indicate either a basal defect in the antiviral response in NINL KO cells or a second function of NINL that is IFN independent.
evidence: Observed in viral replication data shown in Figure 2B-C comparing untreated WT and NINL KO cells.

claim: NIN KO cells do not show the same attenuation of IFN antiviral potency as NINL KO cells.
source: Each virus was sensitive to the antiviral effect of IFN in WT and NIN KO cells, although the degree of sensitivity was different for each virus as would be expected due to known differences in viral sensitivity to different ISGs (Schoggins et al., 2014; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D). However, with both SinV and CVB3, as we observed with VSV, the antiviral effect of IFN was reduced in NINL KO cells compared to WT or NIN KO cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by viral replication assays showing similar IFN responses in WT and NIN KO cells, but reduced IFN response in NINL KO cells across multiple viruses (Figure 2B-D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: NINL KO cells have robust phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT2 in response to IFNα pretreatment.
source: Despite robust phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT2 in response to IFNα pretreatment in WT, NINL KO, and NIN KO cells, protein expression of the canonical ISGs–MX1, IFIT3, OAS1, and ISG15 was greatly reduced in NINL KO cells relative to WT or NIN KO cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis showing pSTAT1(Y701) and pSTAT2(Y690) in NINL KO cells after IFNα treatment (Figure 3A).

claim: Protein expression of canonical ISGs (MX1, IFIT3, OAS1, and ISG15) is greatly reduced in NINL KO cells relative to WT or NIN KO cells after IFNα treatment.
source: Despite robust phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT2 in response to IFNα pretreatment in WT, NINL KO, and NIN KO cells, protein expression of the canonical ISGs–MX1, IFIT3, OAS1, and ISG15 was greatly reduced in NINL KO cells relative to WT or NIN KO cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis showing reduced ISG protein levels in NINL KO cells compared to WT and NIN KO cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: 88 ISGs were significantly upregulated in response to IFN treatment in WT A549 cells.
source: In WT cells, we identified 88 ISGs that were significantly (adjusted p-value≤0.05, log2-fold change ≥ 1) upregulated in response to IFN treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Identified by RNAseq analysis of WT A549 cells with and without IFNα treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).

claim: Many ISG transcripts from IFNα-treated NINL KO cells are downregulated compared to IFNα-treated WT cells.
source: Consistent with our western blot analysis, the induction pattern of ISG transcripts in WT and NIN KO cells was similar, whereas many ISG transcripts from IFNα-treated NINL KO cells were downregulated compared to IFNα-treated WT cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis comparing ISG expression between cell lines (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3-4, Supplementary file 4).

claim: VacV J3 mutant replication is significantly reduced upon IFNα pretreatment in WT and NIN KO A549 cells, but not in NINL KO cells.
source: As expected, in WT and NIN KO A549 cells, wild-type VacV (VacV WT) was insensitive to IFNα, whereas VacV J3 replication was significantly reduced upon IFNα pretreatment (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A). In contrast, mutant and wild-type viruses replicated equivalently in the NINL KO cells regardless of IFNα pretreatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by viral replication assays comparing VacV WT and J3 mutant in WT, NIN KO, and NINL KO cells with and without IFNα pretreatment (Figure 3C-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).

claim: The VacV J3 mutant is sensitized to the antiviral effects of IFIT family ISGs due to a point mutation in the J3 methyltransferase protein.
source: However, a point mutation in the J3 methyltransferase protein (VacV J3) confers interferon sensitivity by sensitizing the virus to the antiviral effects of the IFIT family of ISGs (Daffis et al., 2010; Daugherty et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2018; Latner et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing the VacV J3 mutant.

claim: IFIT1, IFIT2, and IFIT3 are among the ISGs decreased in NINL KO cells relative to WT and NIN KO cells.
source: As IFIT1, IFIT2, and IFIT3 were among the ISGs we saw decreased in NINL KO cells relative to WT and NIN KO cells (Supplementary file 4), we hypothesized that NINL KO cells may lack the ability to inhibit the J3 mutant VacV after IFNα pretreatment.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: pSTAT1 shows significantly reduced nuclear localization in NINL KO cells compared to WT and NIN KO cells after IFNα treatment.
source: This analysis revealed that pSTAT1 shows significantly reduced nuclear localization in NINL KO cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy and quantification of nuclear to cytoplasmic fluorescence intensity ratios of pSTAT1 (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: In WT and NIN KO cells, pretreatment with IFNα leads to translocation of pSTAT1 to the nucleus.
source: In both WT and NIN KO cells, pretreatment with IFNα led to the translocation of pSTAT1 to the nucleus as expected (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing nuclear pSTAT1 localization in WT and NIN KO cells after IFNα treatment (Figure 4A).

claim: In NINL KO cells, pSTAT1 shows diffuse cytoplasmic staining after treatment with IFNα.
source: In contrast, in NINL KO cells we observed diffuse cytoplasmic staining of pSTAT1 after treatment with IFNα (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy showing cytoplasmic pSTAT1 localization in NINL KO cells after IFNα treatment (Figure 4A).

claim: NINL is implicated in the trafficking of the pSTAT1 transcription factor to the nucleus.
source: These data implicate NINL in the trafficking of the pSTAT1 transcription factor to the nucleus (Figure 4C).
evidence: Inferred from data showing reduced nuclear localization of pSTAT1 in NINL KO cells (Figure 4A-B) and NINL's known role as a dynein activating adaptor involved in intracellular transport.

claim: CVB3 3Cpro cleaves human NINL at three sites: residues 231, 827, and 1032.
source: Using a predictive model of enteroviral 3C protease (3Cpro) target specificity (Tsu et al., 2021a), we identified three high-confidence sites of potential cleavage within NINL at residues 231, 827, and 1032 (Figure 5A) in which amino acid diversity within primates is expected to alter 3Cpro cleavage susceptibility (Figure 5B). Indeed, upon transfection of NINL and CVB3 3Cpro into HEK293T cells, which were used for their ease of transfection and protein expression, we observed an overall reduction of full-length NINL and the appearance of two cleavage products at sizes that correspond to predicted cleavage at sites 827 and 1032 (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by predictive modeling (Tsu et al., 2021a) and cleavage assays showing cleavage products corresponding to sites 231, 827, and 1032 (Figure 5A-D). Site specificity confirmed by point mutations preventing cleavage (Figure 5D).

claim: Amino acid diversity at NINL cleavage sites within primates is expected to alter 3Cpro cleavage susceptibility.
source: Using a predictive model of enteroviral 3C protease (3Cpro) target specificity (Tsu et al., 2021a), we identified three high-confidence sites of potential cleavage within NINL at residues 231, 827, and 1032 (Figure 5A) in which amino acid diversity within primates is expected to alter 3Cpro cleavage susceptibility (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment showing variation at cleavage sites across primate species (Figure 5B) and predictive modeling based on known 3Cpro specificity.

claim: NINL point mutants replacing glutamine with arginine at the P1 position prevent cleavage by CVB3 3Cpro.
source: Specifically, we replaced the glutamine immediately preceding the site of cleavage (the P1 position) with an arginine found in non-human primates that we predicted would prevent cleavage by 3Cpros (Tsu et al., 2021a) for each of the predicted sites. Co-transfection of CVB3 3Cpro with NINL containing these mutations individually (Q1032R) or in combination (double mutant Q827R/Q1032R [Double] and triple mutant Q231R/Q827R/Q1032R [Triple]) confirmed the sites of cleavage, with the NINL triple mutant eliminating all cleavage products by CVB3 3Cpro (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays showing that NINL triple mutant (Q231R/Q827R/Q1032R) eliminates all cleavage products by CVB3 3Cpro (Figure 5D).

claim: Two NINL cleavage sites (Q827 and Q1032) reside in exon 17 within the carboxy-terminal region of NINL.
source: We also noted that two of these sites (Q827 and Q1032), along with many of the codons predicted to be evolving under positive selection (Figure 1C), reside in a single exon (exon 17) within the carboxy-terminal region of NINL (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated directly in the text and shown in Figure 5A schematic.

claim: NINL isoform 2 lacks exon 17.
source: Intriguingly, this exon is lacking in an alternatively spliced isoform of NINL (isoform 2) (Dona et al., 2015; Kersten et al., 2012; van Wijk et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing NINL isoforms.

claim: NINL isoform 2 shows minimal cleavage by CVB3 3Cpro compared to isoform 1.
source: Consistent with the loss of two primary sites of cleavage, we observed minimal decrease in the full-length product when isoform 2 was co-transfected with CVB3 3Cpro, although we did observe weak protease-mediated cleavage at site 231 in isoform 2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays comparing isoform 1 and isoform 2 cleavage by CVB3 3Cpro (Figure 5D).

claim: All picornavirus 3Cpros tested are able to cleave NINL to some degree, but with variable strength and position of cleavage.
source: Interestingly, while we found that all proteases tested were able to cleave NINL to some degree, the strength and position of cleavage was variable, even among proteases from closely related viruses such CVB3, enterovirus 71 (EV71), poliovirus (PV1), enterovirus D68 (EV68), and human rhinovirus A (HRVA), all of which are members of the enterovirus genus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays with a panel of 3Cpros from diverse picornaviruses showing variable cleavage patterns (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Coronavirus 3CLpros from SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, and NL63-CoV cleave NINL at multiple sites, some of which map to residues 827 and 1032.
source: We also tested a panel of 3C-like proteases (3CLpros) from members of the Coronaviridae family, including proteases from the betacoronaviruses, SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV, and an alphacoronavirus, NL63-CoV. We again observed numerous cleavage products, some of which map to residues 827 and 1032 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with 3Cpros and 3CLpros having similar active sites and cleavage preferences (Ng et al., 2021).
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays with coronavirus 3CLpros showing cleavage products (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). Similarity to 3Cpro cleavage supported by citation.

claim: 3Cpros and 3CLpros have similar active sites and cleavage preferences.
source: We again observed numerous cleavage products, some of which map to residues 827 and 1032 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with 3Cpros and 3CLpros having similar active sites and cleavage preferences (Ng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ng et al., 2021.

claim: Host- and virus-specificity of NINL cleavage is a hallmark of host–virus arms races.
source: Together, these data indicate that NINL is cleaved at species-specific sites by various proteases from human viruses. Such host- and virus-specificity of cleavage is a hallmark of host–virus arms races (Tsu et al., 2021b), further supporting the model that NINL's role in the interferon response positions it in evolutionary conflict with viruses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsu et al., 2021b describing characteristics of host-virus arms races.

claim: CVB3 infection cleaves NINL at species-specific sites 231, 827, and 1032.
source: Consistent with the results we obtained with transfected 3Cpros, we observed cleavage of NINL at species-specific sites 231, 827, and 1032 when we infected with CVB3, and little to no cleavage upon EMCV infection (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection-based cleavage assays showing NINL cleavage during CVB3 infection (Figure 5E).

claim: EMCV infection results in little to no cleavage of NINL.
source: Consistent with the results we obtained with transfected 3Cpros, we observed cleavage of NINL at species-specific sites 231, 827, and 1032 when we infected with CVB3, and little to no cleavage upon EMCV infection (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection-based cleavage assays showing minimal NINL cleavage during EMCV infection (Figure 5E).

claim: NINL is a centrosome-associated protein.
source: NINL is well known as a centrosome-associated protein and may also be involved in trafficking endo/lysosomal membranes (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing NINL localization and function.

claim: NINL may be involved in trafficking endo/lysosomal membranes.
source: NINL is well known as a centrosome-associated protein and may also be involved in trafficking endo/lysosomal membranes (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies suggesting this function.

claim: Rapalog-induced heterodimerization of NINL-FRB and PEX3-FKBP causes peroxisomes to redistribute to the centrosome in U-2 OS cells.
source: When we introduced these constructs into human U-2 OS cells, taking advantage of their flat epithelial-like morphology that is ideal for imaging, we found that peroxisomes were distributed throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C), but redistributed to the centrosome upon the addition of the rapamycin analog, rapalog (which induces dimerization of FRB and FKBP; Ho et al., 1996; Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by peroxisome trafficking assays showing centrosomal accumulation of peroxisomes upon rapalog treatment (Figure 6C-E). Mechanism of rapalog-induced dimerization supported by citation.

claim: Co-expression of CVB3 3Cpro prevents NINL-mediated redistribution of peroxisomes to the centrosome.
source: In contrast, when NINL was co-expressed with CVB3 3Cpro, peroxisomes no longer localized to the centrosome (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by peroxisome trafficking assays showing loss of centrosomal peroxisome accumulation when CVB3 3Cpro is co-expressed with NINL (Figure 6C-E).

claim: The uncleavable NINL triple mutant can redistribute peroxisomes in the presence of CVB3 3Cpro as effectively as cells not expressing CVB3 3Cpro.
source: However, the uncleavable NINL triple mutant was still able to redistribute peroxisomes in the presence of CVB3 3Cpro just as effectively as U-2 OS cells not expressing CVB3 3Cpro (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by peroxisome trafficking assays showing that NINL triple mutant maintains peroxisome trafficking function in the presence of CVB3 3Cpro (Figure 6C-E).

claim: CVB3 infection leads to a significant reduction in peroxisomes that localize to the centrosome in cells expressing wild-type NINL, but not in cells expressing the uncleavable NINL triple mutant.
source: Similar to transfection with viral protease, live CVB3 infection led to a significant reduction in peroxisomes that localized to the centrosome in cells expressing NINL, but not in cells expressing the uncleavable NINL triple mutant (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by peroxisome trafficking assays during CVB3 infection showing disruption of NINL-mediated trafficking that is prevented by the triple mutant (Figure 7A-B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Site-specific cleavage of NINL by CVB3 3Cpro disrupts NINL's role in cargo transport.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that site-specific cleavage of NINL by CVB3 3Cpro could disrupt NINL's role in cargo transport.
evidence: Inferred from peroxisome trafficking assays showing that CVB3 3Cpro cleavage prevents NINL-mediated peroxisome transport, while uncleavable mutant maintains function (Figures 6-7).

claim: Around 30% of all adaptive amino acid changes in humans result from viral selective pressure.
source: Compellingly, it is estimated that around 30% of all adaptive amino acid changes in humans result from viral selective pressure (Enard et al., 2016; Enard and Petrov, 2018), suggesting that many host–virus conflicts remain undescribed.
evidence: Supported by citations to Enard et al., 2016 and Enard and Petrov, 2018.

claim: Many host antiviral factors that directly interact with viral proteins display signatures of recurrent positive (diversifying) selection over evolutionary time.
source: Indeed, many host antiviral factors that directly interact with viral proteins display signatures of recurrent positive (diversifying) selection over evolutionary time, and genetic variation in these host–virus interactions shapes species-specific susceptibility to circulating and emerging pathogens (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Duggal and Emerman, 2012; Tenthorey et al., 2022; Meyerson and Sawyer, 2011; Rothenburg and Brennan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies documenting this pattern.

claim: Genetic variation in host–virus interactions shapes species-specific susceptibility to circulating and emerging pathogens.
source: Indeed, many host antiviral factors that directly interact with viral proteins display signatures of recurrent positive (diversifying) selection over evolutionary time, and genetic variation in these host–virus interactions shapes species-specific susceptibility to circulating and emerging pathogens (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Duggal and Emerman, 2012; Tenthorey et al., 2022; Meyerson and Sawyer, 2011; Rothenburg and Brennan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Viruses co-opt the microtubule cytoskeleton for cell entry, transport of viral components to sites of replication, remodeling of cellular compartments, and viral egress.
source: For example, viruses co-opt the microtubule cytoskeleton for cell entry, transport of viral components to sites of replication, remodeling of cellular compartments, and viral egress (Brandenburg and Zhuang, 2007; Dodding and Way, 2011; Döhner et al., 2005; Radtke et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies documenting these viral processes.

claim: The host adaptive and innate immune response require movement of signaling components, transport of endocytic and exocytic vesicles, organelle recycling, and cellular remodeling, all of which require the microtubule-based trafficking machinery.
source: Similarly, in response to infection, the host adaptive and innate immune response require movement of signaling components, transport of endocytic and exocytic vesicles, organelle recycling, and cellular remodeling, all of which require the microtubule-based trafficking machinery (Ilan-Ber and Ilan, 2019; Kast and Dominguez, 2017; Man and Kanneganti, 2016; Mostowy and Shenoy, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies documenting these immune processes.

claim: Only one dynein motor-containing gene, cytoplasmic dynein-1 (DYNC1H1), is responsible for long-distance transport in the cytoplasm in human cells.
source: In human cells, only one dynein motor-containing gene, cytoplasmic dynein-1 (DYNC1H1), is responsible for long-distance transport in the cytoplasm.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the dynein transport system.

claim: The active cytoplasmic dynein-1 complex is composed of multiple dynein subunits, the multisubunit dynactin complex, and one of a growing list of activating adaptors.
source: However, the active cytoplasmic dynein-1 complex (hereafter dynein) is composed of multiple dynein subunits, the multisubunit dynactin complex, and one of a growing list of activating adaptors (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to McKenney et al., 2014 and Schlager et al., 2014.

claim: Activating adaptors provide cargo specificity for dynein in addition to their essential role in activating robust processive motility.
source: Interestingly, it is the activating adaptors that provide cargo specificity for dynein in addition to their essential role in activating robust processive motility (Olenick and Holzbaur, 2019; Reck-Peterson et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Olenick and Holzbaur, 2019 and Reck-Peterson et al., 2018.

claim: The specific biological functions of most activating adaptors remain unknown.
source: However, the specific biological functions of most activating adaptors remain unknown.
evidence: Stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The dynein/dynactin complex is composed of two copies of the ATPase-containing heavy chain, two copies of five additional dynein chains, and the 23-subunit dynactin complex.
source: The dynein/dynactin complex is composed of two copies of the ATPase-containing heavy chain, two copies of five additional dynein chains, the 23-subunit dynactin complex, and an activating adaptor (Olenick and Holzbaur, 2019; Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Each human dynein gene was compared to orthologs in 13–20 diverse simian primates for evolutionary analysis.
source: Each human dynein gene was compared to orthologs in 13–20 diverse simian primates, and a gene-wide dN/dS (also known as omega) value was calculated, which compares the gene-wide rate of nonsynonymous changes (i.e., amino acid altering) to the rate of synonymous (i.e., silent) changes.
evidence: Described in the methods for evolutionary analysis.

claim: NINL showed strong evidence for recurrent positive selection in primates, consistent with previous data.
source: In contrast, NINL showed strong evidence for recurrent positive selection in primates, consistent with previous data (Gordon et al., 2020; Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1), establishing the possibility that NINL could be at the interface of a host–pathogen interaction.
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis data (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1) and citation to Gordon et al., 2020.

claim: The amino-terminal region of NINL (residues 1-702) binds dynein/dynactin.
source: Most (24 of 30) of these codons are excluded from the known dynein/dynactin-binding region of NINL (residues 1–702) (Redwine et al., 2017) and instead are located in the carboxy-terminal region of the protein that is expected to interact with cargo (residues 703–1382).
evidence: Supported by citation to Redwine et al., 2017.

claim: The carboxy-terminal region of NINL (residues 703-1382) is expected to interact with cargo.
source: Most (24 of 30) of these codons are excluded from the known dynein/dynactin-binding region of NINL (residues 1–702) (Redwine et al., 2017) and instead are located in the carboxy-terminal region of the protein that is expected to interact with cargo (residues 703–1382).
evidence: Inferred from the known function of activating adaptors and the location of the domain relative to the dynein/dynactin-binding region.

claim: The amino-terminus of NINL alone shows no evidence for positive selection.
source: When we analyzed individual domains on their own, we found no evidence for positive selection in the amino-terminus alone, while the carboxy-terminus retained a significant signature of positive selection (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by domain-specific evolutionary analyses (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 3).

claim: The carboxy-terminus of NINL retains a significant signature of positive selection when analyzed independently.
source: When we analyzed individual domains on their own, we found no evidence for positive selection in the amino-terminus alone, while the carboxy-terminus retained a significant signature of positive selection (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by domain-specific evolutionary analyses (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 3).

claim: A549 cells are susceptible to infection with many viruses and mount an effective antiviral response after treatment with IFN.
source: To evaluate this hypothesis, we generated a human A549 cell line that lacked NINL (NINL KO) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) as A549 cells are susceptible to infection with many viruses and mount an effective antiviral response after treatment with IFN.
evidence: Stated as rationale for using A549 cells, based on established knowledge of this cell line.

claim: Ninein (NIN) is the closest human paralog to NINL and shares a similar domain architecture.
source: In parallel, we generated cells that lacked ninein (NIN KO) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), the closest human paralog to NINL, which shares a similar domain architecture with NINL and is also a dynein activator adaptor (Redwine et al., 2017), but shows no evidence for positive selection (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Redwine et al., 2017 and evolutionary analysis data (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).

claim: NIN is a dynein activator adaptor.
source: In parallel, we generated cells that lacked ninein (NIN KO) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), the closest human paralog to NINL, which shares a similar domain architecture with NINL and is also a dynein activator adaptor (Redwine et al., 2017), but shows no evidence for positive selection (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Redwine et al., 2017.

claim: NIN shows no evidence for positive selection.
source: In parallel, we generated cells that lacked ninein (NIN KO) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), the closest human paralog to NINL, which shares a similar domain architecture with NINL and is also a dynein activator adaptor (Redwine et al., 2017), but shows no evidence for positive selection (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by evolutionary analysis data (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).

claim: IFNα pretreatment results in a >100-fold decrease in viral replication in WT and NIN KO cells.
source: Consistent with the strong antiviral effect of IFNα, we observed a >100-fold decrease in viral replication in WT and NIN cells that had been pretreated with IFNα (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by VSV replication assays (Figure 2B).

claim: The magnitude of the IFN effect varies between cell types likely due to cell type-specific differences in basal and induced ISG expression.
source: We again observed that NINL KO cells had a significant reduction in the antiviral effects of IFNα pretreatment (Figure 2C), although the magnitude of the IFN effect varied between cell types likely due to cell type-specific differences in basal and induced ISG expression (Rusinova et al., 2013).
evidence: Observed in data comparing A549 and U-2 OS cells, with explanation supported by citation to Rusinova et al., 2013.

claim: Different viruses have different degrees of sensitivity to IFN due to known differences in viral sensitivity to different ISGs.
source: Each virus was sensitive to the antiviral effect of IFN in WT and NIN KO cells, although the degree of sensitivity was different for each virus as would be expected due to known differences in viral sensitivity to different ISGs (Schoggins et al., 2014; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Observed in viral replication data and explained by citation to Schoggins et al., 2014.

claim: The attenuation of the IFN-induced antiviral effect against viruses from three distinct families suggests that NINL may broadly play a role in the IFN-mediated innate immune response to viruses.
source: The attenuation of the IFN-induced antiviral effect against viruses from three distinct families suggests that NINL may broadly play a role in the IFN-mediated innate immune response to viruses.
evidence: Inferred from data showing reduced IFN effect in NINL KO cells across VSV, SinV, and CVB3 from three different viral families.

claim: Type I IFNs activate the JAK/STAT pathway to trigger the expression of ISGs.
source: Type I IFNs, such as IFNα, activate the Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) pathway to trigger the expression of ISGs, which include potent antiviral effectors (Schoggins, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoggins, 2019.

claim: ISGs include potent antiviral effectors.
source: Type I IFNs, such as IFNα, activate the Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) pathway to trigger the expression of ISGs, which include potent antiviral effectors (Schoggins, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoggins, 2019.

claim: The lack of ISG protein expression in NINL KO cells is independent of cell background or the choice of CRISPR guide.
source: To again confirm that this was not specific to cell type, we showed that this lack of ISG protein expression was independent of cell background or the choice of CRISPR guide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis in multiple cell lines and CRISPR clones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The induction pattern of ISG transcripts in WT and NIN KO cells is similar.
source: Consistent with our western blot analysis, the induction pattern of ISG transcripts in WT and NIN KO cells was similar, whereas many ISG transcripts from IFNα-treated NINL KO cells were downregulated compared to IFNα-treated WT cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3-4).

claim: Other transcripts unrelated to the IFN response also show altered expression in NINL KO cells relative to WT cells.
source: Other transcripts unrelated to the IFN response also showed altered expression in NINL KO cells relative to WT cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 4).

claim: The overall lower expression of ISGs in NINL KO relative to WT cells indicates that cells lacking NINL have a distinct defect in their ability to mount an effective antiviral immune response.
source: However, the overall lower expression of ISGs in NINL KO relative to WT cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) indicates that cells lacking NINL have a distinct defect in their ability to mount an effective antiviral immune response.
evidence: Inferred from RNAseq data showing reduced ISG expression in NINL KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

claim: Wild-type VacV is insensitive to IFNα due to the large number of proteins the virus encodes that antagonize the immune response.
source: Vaccinia virus (VacV) is a large double-stranded DNA virus that is relatively insensitive to the effects of IFNα due to the large number of proteins the virus encodes that antagonize the immune response (Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2021.

claim: NINL acts after the phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT2 but before ISG transcription in the IFN signaling cascade.
source: Thus far, our data suggest that NINL acts after the phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT2 (Figure 3A), but before ISG transcription (Figure 3B).
evidence: Inferred from data showing normal STAT phosphorylation but reduced ISG expression in NINL KO cells (Figure 3A-B).

claim: Upon initiation of JAK/STAT signaling, STAT1 and STAT2 are phosphorylated, heterodimerize, and bind to IRF9 to form ISGF3.
source: Upon initiation of JAK/STAT signaling, STAT1 and STAT2 are phosphorylated, heterodimerize, and bind to IFN regulatory factor 9 (IRF9) to form the heterotrimeric interferon-stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3) (Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schneider et al., 2014.

claim: ISGF3 translocates to the nucleus and binds to ISREs found in the promoters of ISGs.
source: ISGF3 then translocates to the nucleus and binds to the IFN-stimulated response elements (ISREs) found in the promoters of ISGs (Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schneider et al., 2014.

claim: Viruses deploy virus-encoded proteases to cleave components of the host antiviral defense system as a viral antagonism strategy.
source: One such viral antagonism strategy is to deploy virus-encoded proteases to cleave components of the host antiviral defense system (Lei and Hilgenfeld, 2017; Tsu et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lei and Hilgenfeld, 2017 and Tsu et al., 2021b.

claim: A predictive model of enteroviral 3Cpro target specificity can identify high-confidence cleavage sites within NINL.
source: Using a predictive model of enteroviral 3C protease (3Cpro) target specificity (Tsu et al., 2021a), we identified three high-confidence sites of potential cleavage within NINL at residues 231, 827, and 1032 (Figure 5A) in which amino acid diversity within primates is expected to alter 3Cpro cleavage susceptibility (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by applying the predictive model from Tsu et al., 2021a to NINL sequence.

claim: HEK293T cells were used for cleavage assays due to their ease of transfection and protein expression.
source: Indeed, upon transfection of NINL and CVB3 3Cpro into HEK293T cells, which were used for their ease of transfection and protein expression, we observed an overall reduction of full-length NINL and the appearance of two cleavage products at sizes that correspond to predicted cleavage at sites 827 and 1032 (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Stated as rationale for cell line choice.

claim: Many codons predicted to be evolving under positive selection in NINL reside in exon 17.
source: We also noted that two of these sites (Q827 and Q1032), along with many of the codons predicted to be evolving under positive selection (Figure 1C), reside in a single exon (exon 17) within the carboxy-terminal region of NINL (Figure 5A).
evidence: Observed by comparing locations of positively selected codons (Figure 1C) with exon structure (Figure 5A).

claim: Infection-mediated cleavage efficiency and specificity of NINL recapitulates results from transiently transfected viral proteases.
source: We next aimed to confirm that infection-mediated cleavage efficiency and specificity recapitulated results we observed from transiently transfected viral proteases.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing transfection-based and infection-based cleavage assays (Figure 5D-E).

claim: EMCV 3Cpro only weakly cleaves NINL at a single site in the N-terminus.
source: Therefore infected cells expressing WT NINL and the NINL triple mutant with CVB3, a virus that encodes a 3Cpro that strongly cleaves NINL at multiple sites, and EMCV, a virus that encodes a 3Cpro that only weakly cleaves NINL at a single site in the N-terminus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays with EMCV 3Cpro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: A number of NINL-interacting proteins have been described.
source: In addition, a number of NINL-interacting proteins have been described (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2015; Casenghi et al., 2003; Dona et al., 2015; Kersten et al., 2012; Redwine et al., 2017; van Wijk et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In the context of the interferon response, a NINL cargo has not yet been identified.
source: However, in the context of the interferon response, we have not yet identified a NINL cargo.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: A heterologous peroxisome trafficking assay can be used to reconstitute NINL's role in dynein-mediated microtubule transport.
source: Thus, we chose to reconstitute NINL's role in dynein-mediated microtubule transport using a heterologous approach (Kapitein et al., 2010; Passmore et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kapitein et al., 2010 and Passmore et al., 2021 describing this approach.

claim: Some activating adaptors are autoinhibited via interactions between their amino- and carboxy-termini.
source: We truncated the NINL constructs at residue 1062 because some activating adaptors are autoinhibited via interactions between their amino- and carboxy-termini (Liu et al., 2013; Terawaki et al., 2015; Urnavicius et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013, Terawaki et al., 2015, and Urnavicius et al., 2015.

claim: U-2 OS cells have a flat epithelial-like morphology that is ideal for imaging.
source: When we introduced these constructs into human U-2 OS cells, taking advantage of their flat epithelial-like morphology that is ideal for imaging, we found that peroxisomes were distributed throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C), but redistributed to the centrosome upon the addition of the rapamycin analog, rapalog (which induces dimerization of FRB and FKBP; Ho et al., 1996; Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Stated as rationale for cell line choice.

claim: Peroxisomes are distributed throughout the cytoplasm in U-2 OS cells expressing NINL-FRB and PEX3-FKBP constructs without rapalog treatment.
source: When we introduced these constructs into human U-2 OS cells, taking advantage of their flat epithelial-like morphology that is ideal for imaging, we found that peroxisomes were distributed throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C), but redistributed to the centrosome upon the addition of the rapamycin analog, rapalog (which induces dimerization of FRB and FKBP; Ho et al., 1996; Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy of peroxisome distribution (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C).

claim: Rapalog induces dimerization of FRB and FKBP.
source: When we introduced these constructs into human U-2 OS cells, taking advantage of their flat epithelial-like morphology that is ideal for imaging, we found that peroxisomes were distributed throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C), but redistributed to the centrosome upon the addition of the rapamycin analog, rapalog (which induces dimerization of FRB and FKBP; Ho et al., 1996; Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ho et al., 1996.

claim: NINL is important for limiting viral infection, especially in the presence of type I interferon.
source: Using NINL knockout (KO) cells, we find that NINL is important for limiting viral infection, especially in the presence of the antiviral signaling cytokine, type I interferon (IFN).
evidence: Demonstrated by viral replication assays showing increased viral replication in NINL KO cells, particularly after IFN treatment (Figure 2).

claim: The attenuation of the antiviral efficacy of IFN in NINL KO cells is due to a dramatic reduction in ISG production.
source: We further demonstrate that this attenuation of the antiviral efficacy of IFN in NINL KO cells is due to a dramatic reduction in interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) production, likely as a consequence of decreased nuclear localization of phosphorylated STAT1 following IFN treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot and RNAseq analyses showing reduced ISG expression (Figure 3) and immunofluorescence showing reduced pSTAT1 nuclear localization (Figure 4).

claim: Decreased nuclear localization of phosphorylated STAT1 following IFN treatment is likely the cause of reduced ISG production in NINL KO cells.
source: We further demonstrate that this attenuation of the antiviral efficacy of IFN in NINL KO cells is due to a dramatic reduction in interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) production, likely as a consequence of decreased nuclear localization of phosphorylated STAT1 following IFN treatment.
evidence: Inferred from data showing reduced pSTAT1 nuclear localization (Figure 4) and reduced ISG expression (Figure 3) in NINL KO cells.

claim: Diverse proteases from picornaviruses and coronaviruses cleave NINL at several host-specific sites.
source: Finally, we show that diverse proteases from picornaviruses and coronaviruses cleave NINL at several host-specific sites, resulting in a disruption of NINL's ability to traffic cargo.
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays with multiple viral proteases showing variable cleavage patterns (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Viral protease cleavage of NINL results in a disruption of NINL's ability to traffic cargo.
source: Finally, we show that diverse proteases from picornaviruses and coronaviruses cleave NINL at several host-specific sites, resulting in a disruption of NINL's ability to traffic cargo.
evidence: Demonstrated by peroxisome trafficking assays showing loss of NINL-mediated transport function after protease cleavage (Figures 6-7).

claim: NINL is a rapidly evolving barrier to viral replication.
source: More broadly, our work implicates a component of the dynein transport machinery as a rapidly evolving barrier to viral replication and highlights the utility of an evolution-guided approach for discovery of new host–virus interactions and the genetic conflicts that may arise from them.
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis showing positive selection (Figure 1) and functional data showing antiviral role (Figures 2-4) and viral antagonism (Figures 5-7).

claim: An evolution-guided approach is useful for discovery of new host–virus interactions and genetic conflicts.
source: More broadly, our work implicates a component of the dynein transport machinery as a rapidly evolving barrier to viral replication and highlights the utility of an evolution-guided approach for discovery of new host–virus interactions and the genetic conflicts that may arise from them.
evidence: Demonstrated by the successful identification of NINL's antiviral function starting from evolutionary signatures of positive selection.

claim: The role of activating adaptors in inducing processive dynein motility was first described in 2014.
source: The role of activating adaptors in inducing processive dynein motility was only described in 2014 (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to McKenney et al., 2014 and Schlager et al., 2014.

claim: The number of established activating adaptors has rapidly expanded since 2014.
source: Since that time, the number of established activating adaptors has rapidly expanded, as has our understanding of the molecular interactions between activating adaptors and dynein/dynactin (Agrawal et al., 2022; Cason et al., 2021; Chaaban and Carter, 2022; Fenton et al., 2021; Lau et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Olenick and Holzbaur, 2019; Reck-Peterson et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: For many activating adaptors, including NINL, much less is known about cargo specificity compared to molecular interactions with dynein/dynactin.
source: However, for many activating adaptors, including NINL, much less is known about cargo specificity.
evidence: Stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: NINL KO cells have a defect in ISG production following IFNα treatment.
source: Our observation that NINL KO cells have a defect in ISG production following IFNα treatment suggests a role for NINL in the IFN signaling pathway.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot and RNAseq analyses (Figure 3).

claim: Recent gene enrichment analyses implicate NINL in several immune pathways, including JAK-STAT signaling.
source: These results are consistent with recent gene enrichment analyses implicating NINL in several immune pathways, including JAK-STAT signaling (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2022.

claim: Whether a signaling complex is a direct cargo of NINL remains to be determined.
source: However, whether a signaling complex is a direct cargo of NINL, or whether NINL's interaction with dynein and dynactin is required for this function, remain to be determined.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of current knowledge and area for future research.

claim: Whether NINL's interaction with dynein and dynactin is required for its function in the IFN response remains to be determined.
source: However, whether a signaling complex is a direct cargo of NINL, or whether NINL's interaction with dynein and dynactin is required for this function, remain to be determined.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of current knowledge and area for future research.

claim: NINL KO cells show several transcriptional changes relative to WT cells beyond ISG expression.
source: Notably, we observe several transcriptional changes in NINL KO cells relative to WT cells, suggesting that NINL plays regulatory roles in the cell beyond our observation of its role in the IFN effect.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis showing differential expression of non-ISG genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 4).

claim: NINL plays regulatory roles in the cell beyond its role in the IFN effect.
source: Notably, we observe several transcriptional changes in NINL KO cells relative to WT cells, suggesting that NINL plays regulatory roles in the cell beyond our observation of its role in the IFN effect.
evidence: Inferred from RNAseq data showing broad transcriptional changes in NINL KO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 4).

claim: Understanding the full range of cargos and biological functions of NINL will require additional studies.
source: Like other activating adaptors, understanding the full range of cargos and biological functions of NINL will require additional studies.
evidence: Stated as a limitation and direction for future research.

claim: Several viruses can antagonize NINL function through proteolytic cleavage.
source: Despite the uncertainty of NINL's mechanistic role in the antiviral immune response, we find that several viruses can antagonize NINL function through proteolytic cleavage.
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays with multiple viral proteases (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and functional assays showing disruption of NINL-mediated transport (Figures 6-7).

claim: Changes within the cleavage sites of NINL in primates suggest that virally encoded proteases are one potential evolutionary pressure driving the rapid evolution of NINL.
source: These changes within the cleavage sites of NINL in primates suggest that virally encoded proteases are one potential evolutionary pressure that is driving the rapid evolution of NINL, similar to other molecular arms races between viral proteases and host proteins (Tsu et al., 2021b).
evidence: Inferred from sequence variation at cleavage sites across primates (Figure 5B) and comparison to known protease-host arms races. Supported by citation to Tsu et al., 2021b.

claim: Even closely related 3Cpros within the enterovirus clade have different site preferences within NINL.
source: Intriguingly, even closely related proteases, for instance, 3Cpros within the enterovirus clade, have different site preferences within NINL, suggesting that viral protease evolution may be shaping its interactions with NINL.
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays showing variable cleavage patterns among enterovirus 3Cpros (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Viral protease evolution may be shaping its interactions with NINL.
source: Intriguingly, even closely related proteases, for instance, 3Cpros within the enterovirus clade, have different site preferences within NINL, suggesting that viral protease evolution may be shaping its interactions with NINL.
evidence: Inferred from observation of variable cleavage patterns among related viral proteases (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: NINL cleavage is almost universally maintained among diverse picornavirus and coronavirus proteases despite a wide array of site preferences and cleavage efficiencies.
source: Indeed, among the diversity of picornavirus and coronavirus proteases we tested, we find that NINL cleavage is almost universally maintained despite a wide array of site preferences and cleavage efficiencies.
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays with multiple viral proteases showing that all tested proteases cleave NINL to some degree (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Numerous viral proteases convergently cleave NINL, reminiscent of other convergently antagonized targets in the innate antiviral response such as MAVS, TRIF, and NEMO.
source: These data indicate that numerous viral proteases convergently cleave NINL, reminiscent of other convergently antagonized targets in the innate antiviral response such as MAVS, TRIF, and NEMO (Tsu et al., 2021b).
evidence: Demonstrated by cleavage assays showing multiple unrelated viral proteases cleave NINL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Comparison to other targets supported by citation to Tsu et al., 2021b.

claim: Cleavage of NINL by 3Cpro during viral infection disrupts NINL-mediated transport of a heterologous cargo.
source: Compellingly, cleavage of NINL by 3Cpro during viral infection disrupts the NINL-mediated transport of a heterologous cargo.
evidence: Demonstrated by peroxisome trafficking assays during CVB3 infection (Figure 7).

claim: Cleavage of NINL could be a host-specific mechanism employed by viruses to disrupt the antiviral immune response and promote their own replicative success.
source: Along with our data indicating that one function of NINL is to potentiate the innate immune response, these data suggest that cleavage of NINL could be a host-specific mechanism employed by viruses to disrupt the antiviral immune response and promote their own replicative success.
evidence: Inferred from data showing NINL's antiviral function (Figures 2-4), host-specific cleavage by viral proteases (Figure 5), and disruption of NINL function by cleavage (Figures 6-7).

claim: This study demonstrates the effectiveness of leveraging genetic signatures of pathogen-driven evolution to identify new components of host innate immunity.
source: Altogether, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of leveraging genetic signatures of pathogen-driven evolution to identify new components of host innate immunity.
evidence: Demonstrated by the successful identification of NINL's antiviral function starting from evolutionary signatures.

claim: Insights into species-specific interactions between viruses and NINL provide a glimpse into the impact that viruses may have on the evolution of the intracellular transport machinery.
source: Our insights into the species-specific interactions between viruses and NINL provides a glimpse into the impact that viruses may have on the evolution of the intracellular transport machinery and identify a new role for a dynein activating adaptor in the antiviral immune response.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary and functional data showing host-specific viral antagonism of NINL.

claim: Components of the otherwise conserved cytoplasmic dynein transport machinery can be engaged in host- and virus-specific interactions.
source: These results indicate that components of the otherwise conserved cytoplasmic dynein transport machinery can be engaged in host- and virus-specific interactions and suggest intracellular transport could be an important battleground for host–virus arms races.
evidence: Demonstrated by data showing NINL is unique among dynein components in evolving under positive selection (Figure 1) and is subject to host- and virus-specific viral antagonism (Figure 5).

claim: Intracellular transport could be an important battleground for host–virus arms races.
source: These results indicate that components of the otherwise conserved cytoplasmic dynein transport machinery can be engaged in host- and virus-specific interactions and suggest intracellular transport could be an important battleground for host–virus arms races.
evidence: Inferred from data showing NINL's role in antiviral immunity and viral antagonism of NINL function.
